title: In an Agent-Based Market (ABM), what should an "agent" actually represent?
author: Serenial_Labs
selftext:
Quick heads-up: I originally wrote this post in my native language and used AI solely to assist with the English translation.

Hi everyone. I’ve been building an agent-based market (ABM) sandbox for financial markets as a personal project. There are already plenty of great backtesters out there, but I wanted to build an ABM because standard backtests lack true participant interaction. You can model slippage or execution fees, but you're never really a market participant impacting other traders—and having those impacts ripple back to you. That feedback loop is what drew me to ABMs in the first place.

Initially, I hacked together a few basic agents in Python to construct a decent-looking market and tested it by paper trading manually. But at some point, reality hit me: *"If this runs in real time, who’s actually going to sit here and play with it? It’s not like it’s making real money."* So I pivoted away from a real-time simulator for human traders toward a logical-time-based sandbox designed for testing quant strategies and AI agents. I’ve sunk a lot of time into building out the core architecture since then.

Once the foundation was solid, though, a bigger issue popped up: reproducing **Stylized Facts (SF)** turned out to be brutally hard. I wanted macro statistical features—fat tails, volatility clustering, the volume-volatility relationship—to emerge naturally from the interactions between agents.

The problem is, the deeper I went down that rabbit hole, the weirder my agents became.

I started out wanting economic actors with clear incentives trying to maximize profit. But as I tweaked behaviors and fine-tuned parameters to force the system to check off each stylized fact, the agents stopped feeling like rational market actors. Instead, they started feeling like artificial props engineered just to sculpt a desired market shape.

That's when I started questioning if I was even heading in the right direction.

* On one hand, you have a market that successfully hits macro-level stylized facts, but where individual agents lack coherent logic and fail to react meaningfully when a user intervenes.
* On the other hand, you have a market that falls short on stylized facts, but features agents with clear objectives and logic that react dynamically to a user's strategy.

Ideally, you'd want both, but in practice, there’s a real tension between the two. And given that my goal isn't to write an academic paper explaining market mechanics, but rather to build an experimental environment where users plug in their own strategies or AI agents to interact with other participants, this trade-off is particularly tricky.

Which form of realism matters more in an ABM? Is it **macro-level statistical realism** (aggregate market characteristics) or **micro-level behavioral realism** (individual agent logic and responsiveness)?

For those who have researched or built financial ABMs, how do you balance this trade-off? I'd love to hear your thoughts or experiences.

comments.author: tradematesHQ
comments.body: You're hitting the classic ABM wall. The stylized facts emerge from heterogeneity and noise, not from rational actors optimizing utility. If you force agents to be too rational, you get efficient markets and no fat tails. If you force the stylized facts, you get agents that are glorified random number generators. The trick is to separate the layers: have agents with coherent micro-level logic, then add a meta-layer of noise traders, herding behavior, and regime-switching that operates on top of them. The fat tails come from the interaction between those layers, not from any single agent. Also, don't overfit to the stylized facts  -  if you tune parameters to hit them exactly, your sandbox becomes a museum piece that can't react to novel strategies.

replies.author: Serenial_Labs
replies.body:
Thanks for the feedback. I think I finally realize where that feeling of friction was coming from while designing this.

It feels like the most balanced architecture is to have individual agents acting on consistent logic to maximize profit, layered beneath separate mechanisms—like herd behavior, noise, or regime shifts—that drive the overall market dynamics.

Separating those two roles clearly, as you pointed out, seems to be the key. Up until now, I was tweaking individual agent behaviors just to force stylized facts into place, and in hindsight, that was exactly what felt so off.

Thanks again, and have a great day!
